newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa govt aims to cut debt to help rates fall.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa govt aims to cut debt to help rates fall.

text.p: The South African government was emphasising a more active management of borrowing to help reduce interest rates and support growth, finance department director general Maria Ramos said on Wednesday.

Briefing the parliamentary finance committee, Ramos noted government's 1997/98 gross borrowing requirement was expected to be 36.9 billion rand but this could be reduced using anticipated privatisation proceeds.

"The market will know upfront what the proceeds are and we will tell the market how much will go back into, for example, Telkom and how much into government coffers and what the likely effect is likely to be on the gross borrowing requirement," she said.
"We will have to look at our own maturity schedule to see what stocks we would want to redeem or retire. Obviously we would want to pick on the most expensive onces in our portfolio."
Analysts expect the imminent sale of a 30 percent stake in Telkom, South Africa's first substantial privatisation deal, to raise some six billion rand.
Ramos said the government would monitor much more closely when large outflows were due and go into the market in time to prevent major disruptions.

"We have to borrow in advance because if we were to go into the market the day before, we would put upward pressure on interest rates. Government is such a big player in this market...so that anything that we do has a direct impact on interest rates," she said.
"So we will have a good sense of when those large cash outflows are going to be and prefund them so that we have a smooth funding pattern."

A new debt management system would initially mainly apply to national government, but provinces and the parastatals, which had limited borrowing powers, would be consulted to maintain a broader picture of national debt.
Foreign borrowings by parastatals would be closely monitored, particularly now that government guarantees were no longer provided free of charge.
This was part of overall plans to improve the financial management of state enterprises so that it was clear what their value was to the state as investments.
